newsitem.title: USA: Dollar leaps as U.S.-Japan trade tensions ebb.
newsitem.headline: Dollar leaps as U.S.-Japan trade tensions ebb.

text.p: The dollar made a spectacular leap of nearly three yen on Thursday after Japanese officials played down signs of trade friction with the United States and chances for an imminent rise in Japan's interest rates.

The dollar had jumped an even more staggering 4-1/2 yen in Asian trade -- from a low of 111.20 yen to a high of 115.70 -- after senior Japanese Ministry of Finance official Eisuke Sakakibara said recent concern over Japan's growing trade surplus with the United States "is being played up excessively".

Sakakibara, believed to be the orchestrator of Japanese foreign exchange policy, also said Japanese interest rates were unlikely to rise soon, as had been speculated in the currency market, given current economic conditions.

"It was the biggest move in dollar-yen since the Iraqi war," said Bob Houck, trader and vice president at Norwest Bank in Minneapolis. "Seeing a 4-1/2 yen move in one session is pretty much unheard of."

The dollar managed to retain most of its gains despite soft May U.S. retail sales data, which suggested Federal Reserve policy-makers may not hike U.S. interest rates at their upcoming July meeting as some had expected.

A sharp rally in U.S. bonds and stocks underpinned the dollar. The Dow Jones industrial average surged to a record high to close up 135.64 points at 7,711.47. The 30-year benchmark U.S. Treasury rose almost a full point, reducing its yield to 6.77 percent from 6.84 percent at Wednesday's close.
The dollar has been exceptionally volatile recently, dealers said, staging an impressive recovery on Thursday after hitting a seven-month low of 110.52 yen the previous day.
The dollar fetched 114.27 yen in late trading, up from 111.15 late Wednesday. It edged up to 1.7290 German marks from 1.7164.
Remarks from U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin and his deputy, Lawrence Summers, failed to give the dollar fresh direction, dealers said.
Rubin repeated recent comments that a sustained rise in Japan's trade suprlus could hurt global growth and spark a protectionist backlash in the United States.
However, he added that there was no sign yet the growth in Japan's trade surplus will be sustained and that the dollar never has and never will be used as a tool to manipulate international trade.

The dollar also edged higher against the mark on speculation that Europe's drive to form a single currency by 1999 would be delayed. The German government was expected to bow to demands from the new French administration to include a commitment to boost jobs in the review of the Maastricht Treaty.
French and German officials meet on Friday in the French town of Poitiers for their regular bilateral summit ahead of the Amsterdam summit of European Union leaders scheduled to begin on Monday.
In other trading, the dollar rose to 1.4435 Swiss francs from 1.4385 but dipped to Canadian $1.3838 from C$1.3871. The British pound slipped to $1.6320 from $1.6380.
